caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Public debt is modest and was the classic counter-cyclical story in miniature: from 17.2% of GDP in 2006 it spiked to 46.4% in 2020 as COVID crushed tourism revenues, then fell to a projected 30.3% in 2025, with the series high at 48.6% in 2021. The economy (GDP of a projected $4.5bn in 2025, from $3.5bn in 2006) is tiny and tourism- and finance-dependent, so ratios move sharply. Andorra joined the IMF in 2020, and fiscal transparency has improved markedly since the banking-tax scandals of the 2010s. Debt is not a sustainability concern at these levels.
inflation_management: Andorra uses the euro unilaterally, so its inflation path is essentially imported from the euro area with a small domestic premium. It was negative in 2009 (-1.2%) during the crisis deflation, then ran low through the 2010s, dipping to 0.1% in 2020. The 2022 energy shock pushed it to 6.2%, the series high, before easing to 3.1% in 2024 and a projected 2.4% in 2025. With no central bank of its own, Andorra has no independent monetary lever; inflation management is fiscal and competitiveness policy by default.

key_events.event: Crisis-driven deflation of -1.2% as tourism and banking activity contracted.
Banking scandal and asset seizures forced a cleanup of the financial sector and stricter transparency rules.
Joined the IMF; COVID-19 collapsed tourism, driving debt to 46.4% of GDP.
Inflation hit 6.2%, the series high, on imported energy and food prices.
Completed an association-agreement negotiation framework with the EU to deepen single-market access.

outlook_next_decade: The outlook is one of stability rather than transformation: low debt, imported price stability, and tourism-led growth. The EU association agreement is the main growth lever, reducing trade frictions over time. Structural risks are over-dependence on tourism and financial services and the lack of monetary autonomy if a shock diverges from the euro-area cycle. On current settings, debt should stay near or below 30% of GDP.
